templates.name: Period between independent clauses (second often opens with an introductory phrase)
Conjunctive adverb: semicolon or period on the correct side, comma on the other
Colon after a complete clause before an explanation or specified item
No punctuation with a restrictive clause or restrictive appositive
Comma plus coordinating conjunction between independent clauses
Items in a series (commas; semicolons when items contain commas)
Comma before a trailing nonrestrictive modifier
No punctuation between subject and verb
No punctuation inside a compound joined by and
No punctuation between a verb or preposition and its object
Question versus statement (word order and end mark)

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses: period before a long past-participle opener
items.passage: In 1937, architectural historians Liang Sicheng and Lin Huiyin went searching for what many scholars considered nonexistent in China: an intact Tang dynasty timber ______ in 857 CE on a remote slope of Mount Wutai, the East Hall of Foguang Temple proved to be one, its age confirmed by an inscription on a roof beam.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The first sentence ends with “an intact Tang dynasty timber building.” The second sentence opens with the participial phrase “Constructed in 857 CE on a remote slope of Mount Wutai,” which describes its subject, “the East Hall of Foguang Temple,” and then gives the verb “proved.” A period correctly separates the two sentences.

A.why_wrong: The comma lets “constructed in 857 CE on a remote slope of Mount Wutai” describe the building, but the main clause “the East Hall of Foguang Temple proved to be one” is then joined to the first main clause with only a comma, a comma splice.

B.why_wrong: “That was constructed ...” keeps the phrase inside the first sentence as a description of the building, so the main clause “the East Hall of Foguang Temple proved to be one” still follows the first main clause with only a comma, a comma splice.

D.why_wrong: With no mark, “building constructed in 857 CE ...” reads as part of the first sentence, and the main clause “the East Hall of Foguang Temple proved to be one” then follows with only a comma, a comma splice.

items.notes: Subject: history and architecture (Foguang Temple East Hall, built 857 CE, identified by Liang Sicheng and Lin Huiyin in 1937). Real subject the writer knows; no fact-check (WAVE.md). Band-7 checks (band7/boundaries.md section 6): past-participle opener of 11 words that reads naturally on clause 1's last noun (“building constructed in 857 CE”); the comma, that-was and glued options hold until the splice at “the East Hall ... proved,” 12 words after the blank; clause 1 ends in a colon-introduced noun phrase, so the boundary falls inside the colon's explanation; one-sentence run of 54 words; cue outside a 6-word window; reasoning steps 3. Key is not the longest option.
band7_moves: past-participle opener of 11 words that could describe clause 1's last noun
the comma, that-was and glued options hold until the splice 12 words after the blank
clause 1 ends in a colon-introduced noun phrase; one-sentence run of 54 words

band7.why: 11-word past-participle opener (“Constructed in 857 CE on a remote slope of Mount Wutai”) reads naturally on “building”; the comma, glued and that-was options hold until “the East Hall ... proved,” 12 words on (ba8ebf49, a872c60a menu); 54-word run.

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses: period before a long noun-phrase opener with internal commas
items.passage: After decades as a lawyer and politician, Uruguayan artist Pedro Figari devoted himself to painting in his sixties, producing hundreds of small ______ scenes of candombe dances, country weddings, and crowded colonial courtyards, these works were painted largely from memory, recalling the Montevideo of Figari’s youth.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The first sentence ends with “producing hundreds of small pictures.” The second sentence opens with the noun phrase “Lively scenes of candombe dances, country weddings, and crowded colonial courtyards,” which describes its subject, “these works,” and then gives the verb “were painted.” A period correctly separates the two sentences.

A.why_wrong: The comma makes “lively scenes of candombe dances ...” an appositive describing the pictures in the first sentence, so the main clause “these works were painted largely from memory” is joined to the first main clause with only the comma after “courtyards,” a comma splice.

B.why_wrong: With no mark, “pictures lively scenes” runs two noun phrases together, and the main clause “these works were painted largely from memory” still follows the first main clause with only a comma, a comma splice.

C.why_wrong: “And lively scenes ...” adds the phrase to what Figari produced in the first sentence, so the main clause “these works were painted largely from memory” is still joined to the first main clause with only a comma, a comma splice.

items.notes: Subject: arts (Pedro Figari, Uruguayan lawyer and politician who moved to Buenos Aires in 1921, at about sixty, to paint full-time; small oils on cardboard of candombe, country life and colonial Montevideo, painted from memory). Real subject the writer knows; no fact-check (WAVE.md). Band-7 checks: noun-phrase opener of 10 words with its own series commas (952fd392 point) that reads as an appositive of clause 1's last noun (“pictures, lively scenes of ...”), as in 0fa289a7 and 940ff6f7; clause 2 renames the same referent (“these works”), as CB's “Ray’s film” does; the splice shows at “these works were painted,” 11 words after the blank; one-sentence run of 46 words; reasoning steps 3. Opener type differs from item 01 (noun phrase vs past participle), and so does the added word (“and” vs “that was”).
band7_moves: noun-phrase opener of 10 words with internal series commas that could describe clause 1's last noun
comma and and-options hold until the splice 11 words after the blank

band7.why: 10-word noun-phrase opener with its own series commas reads as an appositive of “pictures” (940ff6f7, 0fa289a7 pattern); the splice shows only at “these works were painted,” 11 words on.

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses: period before a gerund-phrase subject
items.passage: In 1938, physicist Frank Benford reported that in many real-world data sets, from river areas to city populations, numbers beginning with 1 far outnumber those beginning with any higher ______ whether a company’s accounts follow this pattern, now called Benford’s law, has become a common way for auditors to spot invented figures.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The first sentence ends with “those beginning with any higher digit.” The second sentence’s subject is the gerund phrase “Checking whether a company’s accounts follow this pattern,” and its verb is “has become”; the phrase “now called Benford’s law” sits between them. A period correctly separates the two sentences.

B.why_wrong: The comma attaches “checking whether a company’s accounts follow this pattern” to the first sentence as a modifier, which leaves “has become” without a subject; read as a second main clause instead, it is joined to the first with only a comma, a comma splice.

C.why_wrong: “By checking ...” makes the phrase describe how something in the first sentence happens, which leaves the verb “has become” without a subject.

D.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two main clauses, but “by checking whether a company’s accounts follow this pattern, now called Benford’s law, has become ...” has no subject for “has become.”

items.notes: Subject: social science and statistics (Benford's law: Frank Benford's 1938 paper on leading digits in river areas, populations and other data; now a forensic-accounting check). Real subject the writer knows; no fact-check (WAVE.md). Band-6 shape of 73a6603c: clause 2's subject is a gerund phrase, so the semicolon option adds “by” (a bare semicolon would also be correct; no twin offered); the comma, by and semicolon-by options all leave “has become” without a subject, 12 words after the blank. One-sentence run of 49 words. No band-7 move intended.

band7.why: Gerund-subject shape and menu of band-6 73a6603c; every distractor fails at “has become,” but this is the band-6 move, as planned.

items.subtype: Conjunctive adverb closing clause 1 (L, though; R), contrast with the previous sentence
items.passage: Compiled in the eighth century, the Man’yōshū, Japan’s oldest surviving poetry anthology, is celebrated primarily for verses composed by members of the imperial court. The anthology is not an exclusively aristocratic ______ hundreds of its roughly 4,500 poems are attributed to frontier soldiers, farmers, and other commoners, many of them anonymous.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The first sentence says the Man’yōshū is celebrated primarily for verses by members of the imperial court. “The anthology is not an exclusively aristocratic work, though” qualifies that point, so “though” belongs at the end of this clause, set off by a comma. The semicolon then joins this main clause to the next one, “hundreds of its roughly 4,500 poems are attributed to frontier soldiers, farmers, and other commoners,” which supports it.

A.recipe: semicolon with a non-clause; logic-wrong adverb placement
A.why_wrong: The semicolon leaves “though hundreds of its roughly 4,500 poems are attributed to ...” as a dependent clause standing alone after a semicolon, and it presents the commoners’ poems as a contrast to the claim that the anthology is not exclusively aristocratic, when they support that claim.

C.why_wrong: With “though” heading a subordinate clause, the sentence says the anthology is not exclusively aristocratic even though commoners wrote hundreds of its poems; those poems are the reason for the claim, not a contrast to it.

D.why_wrong: The comma after “though” leaves the two main clauses, “The anthology is not an exclusively aristocratic work” and “hundreds of its roughly 4,500 poems are attributed to ...,” joined by commas alone, a comma splice.

items.notes: Subject: literature (the Man'yoshu, compiled after 759, about 4,500 poems; frontier-guard (sakimori) poems and eastern songs (azuma uta) by commoners, many anonymous). Real subject the writer knows; no fact-check (WAVE.md). Band-7 recipe (band7/boundaries.md section 5): the previous sentence sets an expectation (celebrated for court verses), clause 1 corrects it, clause 2 gives the evidence for clause 1, so neither the semicolon-before-though nor the subordinate-though reading has a contrast to attach to (option menu of 21e58a83 and 5aa171de). Logic-wrong distractors: A and C. Cue outside the window: the previous sentence. Run 27 words, as in the band-7 adverb models.
band7_moves: adverb closes clause 1, which corrects the previous sentence's expectation
clause 2 supports clause 1, so the subordinate-though and semicolon-before-though options fail only on meaning
deciding cue in the previous sentence, outside the blank's window

band7.why: Exact band-7 menu of 21e58a83, 5aa171de, f78997cf: clause 1 qualifies the previous sentence and clause 2 supports it, so “; though” and subordinate “though” fail only on meaning (two logic-wrong distractors, cue in the previous sentence).

items.subtype: Conjunctive adverb opening clause 2 (L; rather, R)
items.passage: From 1974 to 1979, every household in Dauphin, Manitoba, could apply for payments from Mincome, a government experiment that guaranteed a minimum annual income. The project’s designers were not mainly interested in residents’ ______ they wanted to learn whether a guaranteed income would lead people to work less.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “The project’s designers were not mainly interested in residents’ health” and “they wanted to learn whether a guaranteed income would lead people to work less” are both main clauses. A semicolon joins them, and “rather,” set off by a comma, opens the second clause, introducing what the designers did want to study in place of what the first clause rules out.

A.why_wrong: Commas alone around “rather” join the two main clauses, a comma splice.

B.why_wrong: With no mark after “health,” the first main clause runs straight into “rather, they wanted to learn ...,” a run-on sentence.

C.why_wrong: Placing “rather” at the end of the first clause leaves it with nothing to introduce; “rather” presents the replacement idea, so it belongs at the start of the second clause, after the semicolon.

items.notes: Subject: social science (Mincome, Dauphin, Manitoba, 1974-1979, the saturation site where every household could apply; designed to measure work effort, health effects studied only decades later). Real subject the writer knows; no fact-check (WAVE.md). Band-6 adverb shape of a9e5b788 (`; rather,` opens clause 2): key plus comma splice, run-on and the adverb on the wrong side. No band-7 move intended; the adverb's side is decided by the “not” in clause 1.

band7.why: “; rather,” opening clause 2 is the band-6 shape (a9e5b788); band 7 never uses rather. Strong band 6 as planned.

items.subtype: Colon after a complete clause before a noun phrase that specifies it
items.passage: Long known primarily for its intricately carved jade, the Liangzhu culture, which flourished in China’s Yangtze River delta some 5,000 years ago, is now also recognized for a very different kind of ______ extensive system of earthen dams that controlled floodwaters descending from the forested hills north of its walled city.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The main clause “the Liangzhu culture ... is now also recognized for a very different kind of achievement” is complete, and what follows, “an extensive system of earthen dams that controlled floodwaters ...,” is a noun phrase naming that achievement. A colon correctly introduces a phrase that specifies something in the preceding clause.

B.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two main clauses, but “an extensive system of earthen dams that controlled floodwaters ...” is a noun phrase: “controlled” belongs to the relative clause “that controlled floodwaters,” not to a main clause.

C.why_wrong: The period makes “An extensive system of earthen dams that controlled floodwaters ...” a sentence of its own, but it has no main verb (“controlled” belongs to the relative clause), so it is a fragment.

D.why_wrong: “It was an extensive system ...” is a main clause, so joining it to the first main clause with only a comma creates a comma splice.

items.notes: Subject: history and archaeology (Liangzhu culture, Yangtze delta, about 3300-2300 BCE: walled city and a system of earthen dams about 5,000 years old; long known for jade). Real subject the writer knows; no fact-check (WAVE.md). Band-7 recipe (S2_colon): a complete clause ending in an announcing phrase (“a very different kind of achievement”); the noun phrase after the colon carries a relative clause with a finite verb (“that controlled”), so the semicolon and period options look like clause joints (0b005ae2, e9aee0d8 point); comma plus “it was an” as in e9aee0d8. No lone-dash option. Frame differs from e9aee0d8 (no “something far more X” lead-in, no “that, [participle],” clause). One-sentence run of 50 words.
band7_moves: noun phrase after the colon holds a relative clause with a finite verb, so semicolon and period options look like clause joints
comma plus added “it was an” splice option

band7.why: e9aee0d8 menu: announcing phrase, then a noun phrase whose relative clause holds the finite verb “controlled,” so semicolon and period read as clause joints; 50-word run. The announcing phrase makes the colon as visible as in the official, no more.

items.subtype: No punctuation: restrictive title before a name
items.passage: Take almost any four-digit number, arrange its digits in descending and then in ascending order, and subtract the smaller of the two resulting numbers from the larger. Repeating this procedure inevitably yields 6174 within seven iterations, a property described in 1949 by Indian ______ D. R. Kaprekar, a schoolteacher in the town of Devlali.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: In “Indian mathematician D. R. Kaprekar,” the title “Indian mathematician” and the name work together as one unit: the name is needed to say which mathematician is meant, so no punctuation separates them. The comma after “Kaprekar” is already in place, setting off the description “a schoolteacher in the town of Devlali.”

A.why_wrong: A comma between “mathematician” and “D. R. Kaprekar” treats the name as extra information, but the name is essential to identifying the mathematician, so no comma belongs between the title and the name.

B.why_wrong: A colon must follow a complete main clause, and “a property described in 1949 by Indian mathematician” is not one; the colon also splits the title from the name it introduces.

D.why_wrong: A semicolon joins two main clauses, but neither “Repeating this procedure ... by Indian mathematician” nor “D. R. Kaprekar, a schoolteacher in the town of Devlali” forms a main clause the semicolon could link.

items.notes: Subject: mathematics, science (Kaprekar's constant: subtracting the ascending from the descending arrangement of a four-digit number with at least two different digits reaches 6174 in at most seven steps; D. R. Kaprekar, a schoolteacher in Devlali, 1949). Real subject the writer knows; no fact-check (WAVE.md). Band-6 shape of 594b4a94 (title before the blank, name and its nonrestrictive appositive after it, single-mark options). Article-less “Indian mathematician” keeps the restrictive reading certain. No band-7 move intended.

band7.why: 594b4a94 shape: one slot, title before the blank, name and appositive after; local cue. Strong band 6 as planned.

items.subtype: No punctuation: restrictive title and name inside a long subject, then the verb
items.passage: Most antibacterial coatings work by releasing chemicals that poison microbes. In a 2012 study, however, a team led by ______ the wings of an Australian cicada destroy bacteria by purely physical means: microscopic pillars covering the wing’s surface stretch and rupture the cells that settle on them.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Biophysicist Elena Ivanova” is a title followed by the name it identifies, so no punctuation separates them, and no comma belongs around the name. The whole phrase “a team led by biophysicist Elena Ivanova” is the subject of the verb “showed,” and no punctuation should come between a subject and its verb or between “showed” and its object, “that the wings ... destroy bacteria.”

A.why_wrong: The commas set off “Elena Ivanova” as if the name were extra information, but without it “biophysicist” would not say who led the team; the name is essential and takes no commas.

C.why_wrong: The comma after “Ivanova” separates the subject, “a team led by biophysicist Elena Ivanova,” from its verb, “showed.”

D.why_wrong: The comma between “biophysicist” and “Elena Ivanova” splits a title from the name it identifies.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (wings of the clanger cicada, Psaltoda claripennis, kill Pseudomonas aeruginosa mechanically with nanopillars; Ivanova et al. 2012, Swinburne University). Real study and researcher the writer knows; no fact-check (WAVE.md). Band-7 recipe (S4_restrictive): title + name followed by more material that tempts a comma (the verb of a 9-word subject), with a second slot after the name, as in 0a114526's menu (`critic, Stina Chyn, claims` / `critic Stina Chyn, claims,`); article-less “microbiologist” keeps the restrictive reading certain. Exempt from the local-window check (band7/boundaries.md section 6). Reviewer: checked Ivanova et al., Small 2012 (PubMed 22674670: first and corresponding author, nanopillars on cicada wings kill P. aeruginosa, “mechanical rupture”) and her Wikipedia page (led the project; cells on Psaltoda claripennis wings “stretched and ruptured by the nanopillar arrays”; described as a nanobiotechnologist/biophysicist).
band7_moves: title + name inside a long subject, followed by its verb, so a comma after the name tempts
second slot varies with the first (commas around the name, comma before the verb, comma after the title)

fixes: title “microbiologist” changed to “biophysicist” (both supported; the fetched Wikipedia page's headline label), in all four options and the explanations
“a common Australian cicada” to “an Australian cicada” (the fetched species page says endemic, not common)

band7.why: Two-slot menu of 5aae2475 and 0a114526: the name sits inside a 9-word subject right before “showed,” so a comma after the name tempts; S4_restrictive is local at every band, so no window test applies.

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses: comma plus and before an introductory phrase
items.passage: Economist Kate Raworth’s 2017 book Doughnut Economics depicts a sustainable economy as a ring: a zone that meets everyone’s basic needs without exceeding the planet’s ecological limits. In April 2020, Amsterdam formally adopted the ______ within a year, several other cities had begun developing similar plans.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “In April 2020, Amsterdam formally adopted the framework” and “within a year, several other cities had begun developing similar plans” are both main clauses. A comma followed by the coordinating conjunction “and” correctly joins them.

A.why_wrong: When a coordinating conjunction joins two main clauses this long, a comma is conventionally placed before it; here “and within a year” also reads at first as more of the first clause, until “several other cities had begun” arrives.

B.why_wrong: A comma alone cannot join the two main clauses; the result is a comma splice.

C.why_wrong: With no punctuation or conjunction, the two main clauses are fused into a run-on sentence.

items.notes: Subject: social science (Kate Raworth, Doughnut Economics, 2017; Amsterdam formally embraced the model in April 2020, and other cities followed with their own versions). Real subject the writer knows; no fact-check (WAVE.md). Band-6 shape of 59094d87 and 7ce4ee13 (the only hard comma-conjunction officials): clause 2 opens with an introductory phrase (“within a year,”), so the plain comma and the comma-less “and” both look natural. S1_comma_conj has no band-7 officials, so band 6 as planned.

band7.why: S1_comma_conj has no band-7 officials; strong band 6 on 7ce4ee13 and 59094d87, with “within a year,” making the comma-less “and” read naturally.

items.subtype: Complex series: semicolons between items that contain commas
items.passage: The Panchatantra, a collection of animal fables originally composed in Sanskrit, reached readers far beyond India through successive translations. These include a sixth-century Middle Persian version, now ______ Kalila wa-Dimna, completed by the writer Ibn al-Muqaffa around 750 CE; and a Castilian Spanish version dating from 1251.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The sentence lists three translations, and because the items themselves contain commas (“now lost,” “Kalila wa-Dimna, completed by ...”), semicolons separate the items, as the “; and” before the last item shows. A semicolon after “lost” ends the first item, and a comma after “version” begins the phrase “Kalila wa-Dimna, completed by the writer Ibn al-Muqaffa around 750 CE,” which names and describes the Arabic version.

B.why_wrong: A comma after “lost” fails to mark the end of the first item; since the items contain commas and the last one is introduced by “; and,” the items must be separated by semicolons.

C.why_wrong: A colon after “lost” would introduce an explanation of the Middle Persian version instead of separating it from the next item in the series.

D.recipe: series errors (semicolon in the wrong slot)
D.why_wrong: The semicolon after “version” separates “an Arabic version” from its own name, “Kalila wa-Dimna,” while the comma after “lost” fails to mark the end of the first item.

items.notes: Subject: literature (Panchatantra: Burzoy's sixth-century Middle Persian translation, lost; Ibn al-Muqaffa's Arabic Kalila wa-Dimna, about 750; Old Spanish Calila e Dimna, 1251). Real subject the writer knows; no fact-check (WAVE.md). Band-6 shape of 78b88c04 (two slots: semicolon position and comma before the name of the item); the revealing “; and” comes 13 words after the blank.

band7.why: Two-slot shape of band-6 78b88c04; the revealing “; and” comes 13 words after the blank. Strong band 6 as planned.

items.subtype: Comma before a trailing absolute phrase
items.passage: For centuries, Swedish and Norwegian farm families moved their cattle and goats each summer to remote pastures high in the mountains, returning to the valleys in autumn. The women who tended the animals there summoned them home using kulning, a high-pitched, piercing style of ______ notes reverberating across the surrounding valleys and forests.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The main clause “The women who tended the animals there summoned them home using kulning, a high-pitched, piercing style of song” is followed by the absolute phrase “its notes reverberating across the surrounding valleys and forests,” which has no main verb (“reverberating” is a participle). A comma correctly attaches this supplementary phrase to the main clause.

A.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two main clauses, but “its notes reverberating across the surrounding valleys and forests” has no main verb, so it cannot stand on its own after a semicolon.

B.why_wrong: “And” would coordinate the main clause with “its notes reverberating ...,” which is not a clause (it has no main verb), so the two parts are not parallel.

D.why_wrong: The period makes “Its notes reverberating across the surrounding valleys and forests” a sentence of its own, but it has no main verb, so it is a fragment.

items.notes: Subject: arts and music (kulning, the high herding call used by women at Scandinavian summer farms (fabod, seter) to call cattle and goats). Real subject the writer knows; no fact-check (WAVE.md). S2_trailing has no band-6 officials; written as a plain hard item on the 62120607 menu (`quilts, and the` / `quilts, the` / `quilts; the` / `quilts. The`) with a plain absolute phrase (no finite verb inside it, the band-6 version of the trap).

band7.why: Uses band-7 62120607's menu, but the participle “reverberating” just after the blank shows the non-clause plainly; strong band 6 as planned.

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses: comma plus and
items.passage: In most winters, a band of cool water extends northeast along South Africa’s eastern coastline, between the shore and the considerably warmer Agulhas Current. Huge shoals of sardines travel within this band in a migration known as the Sardine ______ dolphins, sharks, and seabirds called Cape gannets follow the shoals, feeding continuously as they go.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Huge shoals of sardines travel within this band in a migration known as the Sardine Run” and “dolphins, sharks, and seabirds called Cape gannets follow the shoals” are both main clauses. A comma followed by the coordinating conjunction “and” correctly joins them.

A.why_wrong: When a coordinating conjunction joins two main clauses this long, a comma is conventionally placed before it.

C.why_wrong: A comma alone cannot join the two main clauses; the result is a comma splice.

D.why_wrong: With no punctuation or conjunction, the two main clauses are fused into a run-on sentence.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (the Sardine Run: in winter, sardine shoals move northeast along South Africa's Eastern Cape and KwaZulu-Natal coasts in a cool inshore band, followed by dolphins, sharks and Cape gannets). Real subject; no fact-check (WAVE.md). Reviewer replacement: the writer's subject (Atacama flowering desert) overlapped official TSP 8bc66f89 (Atacama plant life, seeds hard to germinate) and four live Atacama items. Medium shape: the standard comma-conjunction menu (key, conjunction without comma, splice, fused); the series after the blank keeps the comma-only option tempting.

fixes: subject replaced (Atacama flowering desert overlapped official TSP 8bc66f89 and four live Atacama items): new Sardine Run passage, same menu and key letter, claims.txt withdrawal and new claim appended

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses: comma plus but
items.passage: In 1930, the closing of a textile mill left most families in Marienthal, a village near Vienna, Austria, without work. Such hardship might have been expected to push residents toward political ______ a team of sociologists who studied the village found mostly resignation instead, with residents even borrowing fewer books from the free library.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Such hardship might have been expected to push residents toward political protest” and “a team of sociologists who studied the village found mostly resignation instead” are both main clauses. A comma followed by the coordinating conjunction “but” correctly joins them and signals the contrast between what was expected and what was found.

A.why_wrong: A comma alone cannot join the two main clauses; the result is a comma splice.

B.why_wrong: With no punctuation or conjunction, the two main clauses are fused into a run-on sentence.

C.why_wrong: The comma belongs before “but,” not after it; with no comma before the conjunction and a stray comma after it, the clauses are not joined conventionally.

items.notes: Subject: social science (the Marienthal study, Jahoda, Lazarsfeld and Zeisel, 1933: after the mill closed, residents grew resigned rather than radical; library loans fell although borrowing was free). Real subject the writer knows; no fact-check (WAVE.md). Researchers left unnamed. Medium menu with the comma-after-conjunction decoy (1.26, 2.17 pattern).

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses: period before a short introductory phrase
items.passage: Scattered across the Italian island of Sardinia are the remains of approximately 7,000 nuraghi, cone-shaped towers that were built of huge stone blocks set in place without mortar during the Bronze ______ this day, archaeologists debate whether the towers served as fortresses, as residences, or as places where a community could gather.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The first sentence ends with “during the Bronze Age.” The second sentence begins with the introductory phrase “To this day,” followed by its subject, “archaeologists,” and verb, “debate.” A period correctly separates the two sentences.

B.why_wrong: The comma joins the main clause “archaeologists debate whether the towers served ...” to the first main clause with only a comma, a comma splice.

C.why_wrong: With no mark, “to this day” attaches to the first sentence (“built ... during the Bronze Age to this day”), and the main clause “archaeologists debate ...” then follows with only a comma, a comma splice.

D.why_wrong: “Which to this day” begins a relative clause that is never completed, so the main clause “archaeologists debate ...” is left attached to the first sentence by a comma, and the sentence is not grammatical.

items.notes: Subject: history and archaeology (nuraghi, Bronze Age dry-stone towers of Sardinia, some 7,000 surviving; purpose debated). Real subject the writer knows; no fact-check (WAVE.md). Medium shape: a 3-word opener (“To this day,”) after the period, as in 2.7 and 2.9; the added-word option uses “which” (2.10 menu).

items.subtype: Comma before a trailing participial phrase
items.passage: The orchid mantis, a predatory insect whose legs look like pink and white petals, was long thought to lie camouflaged among orchids to ambush unsuspecting prey. In 2014, however, researchers found that the mantis is itself the lure: it attracts pollinating insects more effectively than many real ______ drawing bees and flies within striking range.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The main clause “it attracts pollinating insects more effectively than many real flowers” is followed by the participial phrase “drawing bees and flies within striking range,” which describes a result of the main clause. A comma correctly separates this supplementary phrase from the main clause.

A.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two main clauses, but “drawing bees and flies within striking range” is a participial phrase with no subject or main verb.

B.why_wrong: The period makes “Drawing bees and flies within striking range” a sentence of its own, but it has no subject or main verb, so it is a fragment.

D.why_wrong: “And” would coordinate the main clause with “drawing bees and flies within striking range,” which is not a clause, so the two parts are not parallel.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (orchid mantis, Hymenopus coronatus: not camouflaged among orchids but a lure that attracts pollinators more than many flowers do; O'Hanlon, Holwell and Herberstein 2014). Real study the writer knows; no fact-check (WAVE.md); researchers unnamed. Medium menu of 2.26 with “and” in place of the missing-comma option (the bare participle could read as modifying “flowers”).

items.subtype: Comma after an introductory participial phrase that contains a restrictive name
items.passage: Mbalax, Senegal’s most popular dance music, blends electric guitars and keyboards with the rhythms of the sabar, a traditional drum. Brought to international audiences in the 1980s by ______ the style remains a fixture of Senegalese weddings, nightclubs, and radio.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: singer Youssou N’Dour, and his band
singer Youssou N’Dour and his band,
singer Youssou N’Dour and his band
singer, Youssou N’Dour and his band
items.explanation: “Brought to international audiences in the 1980s by singer Youssou N’Dour and his band” is an introductory participial phrase describing the subject of the main clause, “the style.” A comma correctly separates the phrase from the main clause, and no punctuation is needed inside the phrase.

A.recipe: comma intrudes into a unit; missing required mark
A.why_wrong: The comma splits the pair “Youssou N’Dour and his band,” and no comma follows the introductory phrase, so “his band the style remains” runs together.

C.why_wrong: Without a comma after the introductory phrase, “his band” runs straight into the main clause, “the style remains a fixture ...”

D.recipe: comma intrudes into a unit; missing required mark
D.why_wrong: The comma separates the title “singer” from the name “Youssou N’Dour,” and no comma follows the introductory phrase.

items.notes: Subject: arts and music (mbalax: Senegalese popular dance music built on sabar drumming with Western instruments; Youssou N'Dour and his band took it abroad in the 1980s). Real subject the writer knows; no fact-check (WAVE.md). Medium shape of 2.20: a participial introductory phrase whose options shift commas inside it as well as at its end.

items.subtype: No punctuation between a long subject and its verb
items.passage: A derecho is a rapidly advancing line of thunderstorms that generates powerful straight-line winds over hundreds of kilometers. The derecho that crossed Iowa in August 2020 with gusts estimated at up to 140 miles per ______ damaged millions of acres of corn and soybeans, making it one of the costliest thunderstorm events in US history.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the second sentence is the long noun phrase “The derecho that crossed Iowa in August 2020 with gusts estimated at up to 140 miles per hour,” and its verb is “damaged.” No punctuation should separate a subject from its verb.

A.why_wrong: A comma after “hour” separates the subject, “The derecho that crossed Iowa ... per hour,” from its verb, “damaged.”

B.why_wrong: A colon must follow a complete main clause, and “The derecho that crossed Iowa ... per hour” is only the subject; the colon would also cut the subject off from its verb.

C.why_wrong: A single dash after “hour” has no partner and separates the subject from its verb, “damaged.”

items.notes: Subject: natural science (the August 10, 2020 Midwest derecho: estimated gusts up to about 140 mph in Iowa, widespread corn and soybean damage, among the costliest US thunderstorm events). Real event the writer knows; no fact-check (WAVE.md). Medium shape of 2.3 and 2.11: a 17-word subject with a relative clause and a with-phrase before the blank, so a comma feels natural; no comma after “2020” (a comma there would open a pair the blank could close).

items.subtype: No punctuation inside a compound joined by both ... and
items.passage: The Batagaika crater in northeastern Siberia began forming in the 1960s, after the clearing of a forest let the summer sun warm the permafrost beneath it, which began to thaw and collapse. Scientists investigate the crater because of both the speed of its ______ remarkably ancient permafrost exposed in its walls.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The phrase “both the speed of its expansion and the remarkably ancient permafrost exposed in its walls” joins two noun phrases, the two things that draw scientists, with “both ... and.” No punctuation is needed between two elements joined this way.

A.why_wrong: Commas before and after “and” break up the two-part phrase “both the speed of its expansion and the remarkably ancient permafrost,” which needs no punctuation.

B.why_wrong: A comma after “and” separates the conjunction from the second element it joins, “the remarkably ancient permafrost.”

D.why_wrong: A comma before “and” is used to join main clauses or to separate three or more items; here “and” joins just two noun phrases after “both,” so no comma belongs there.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (Batagaika crater, the Batagay megaslump in Yakutia: thaw began after forest clearing in the 1960s; its walls expose permafrost hundreds of thousands of years old). Real subject the writer knows; no fact-check (WAVE.md). Medium shape of 2.23: comma variants around “and” in a two-part object; “both” makes the pairing explicit.

items.subtype: No punctuation between a preposition and its object
items.passage: The Huarochirí Manuscript, compiled around 1600 in the highlands of Peru, is a rare colonial-era account of Andean religious traditions written in Quechua rather than Spanish. Many of its stories describe the conflicts ______ the mountain deity Paria Caca and his rivals.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Between” is a preposition, and its object is “the mountain deity Paria Caca and his rivals.” No punctuation should separate a preposition from its object.

B.why_wrong: A colon must follow a complete main clause, and “Many of its stories describe the conflicts between” is not one; the colon would separate the preposition from its object.

C.why_wrong: A comma after “between” separates the preposition from its object, “the mountain deity Paria Caca and his rivals.”

D.why_wrong: A dash after “between” separates the preposition from its object and has no role in the sentence.

items.notes: Subject: literature and religion (the Huarochiri Manuscript, an anonymous Quechua text of about 1600 on the gods and traditions of Huarochiri province, with the mountain deity Paria Caca and his rivals such as Huallallo Carhuincho). Real subject the writer knows; no fact-check (WAVE.md). Easy shape: preposition and object, three odd marks.

items.subtype: No punctuation between a verb and its object
items.passage: The duduk, a woodwind instrument from Armenia, is traditionally carved from apricot wood. In recent decades, film composers have often ______ its warm, mournful sound in their work, and the music for Gladiator (2000) features the Armenian duduk player Djivan Gasparyan.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: In the main clause, “used” is the verb and “its warm, mournful sound” is its object. No punctuation should separate a verb from its object.

A.why_wrong: A colon must follow a complete main clause, and “film composers have often used” is not complete without its object.

C.why_wrong: A comma after “used” separates the verb from its object, “its warm, mournful sound.”

D.why_wrong: A dash after “used” separates the verb from its object and has no partner or role in the sentence.

items.notes: Subject: arts and music (the Armenian duduk, a double-reed instrument of apricot wood; Djivan Gasparyan played on the Gladiator soundtrack). Real subject the writer knows; no fact-check (WAVE.md). Easy shape: verb and object, three odd marks.

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses: comma plus but
items.passage: Engaruka, in northern Tanzania, contains the ruins of a large farming settlement. For several centuries, its farmers used stone-lined channels to carry water from mountain streams to their ______ by the 1800s the settlement had been abandoned.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “For several centuries, its farmers used stone-lined channels to carry water from mountain streams to their fields” and “by the 1800s the settlement had been abandoned” are both main clauses. A comma followed by the coordinating conjunction “but” correctly joins them.

A.why_wrong: A comma alone cannot join the two main clauses; the result is a comma splice.

B.why_wrong: When a coordinating conjunction joins two main clauses this long, a comma is conventionally placed before it.

C.why_wrong: With no punctuation or conjunction, the two main clauses are fused into a run-on sentence.

items.notes: Subject: history and archaeology (Engaruka, below the Rift Valley escarpment in northern Tanzania: stone-lined irrigation channels and terraced fields, farmed for centuries and abandoned during the 1700s). Real subject the writer knows; no fact-check (WAVE.md). Easy shape: the standard comma-conjunction menu.

items.subtype: Comma after an introductory dependent clause
items.passage: The Mabinogion is a collection of eleven medieval Welsh prose tales. Although the stories survive in manuscripts written in the fourteenth ______ of them are thought to be much older, having been passed down by storytellers for generations.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Although the stories survive in manuscripts written in the fourteenth century” is a dependent clause introducing the main clause “many of them are thought to be much older.” A comma correctly separates an introductory dependent clause from the main clause that follows it.

A.why_wrong: The period makes “Although the stories survive in manuscripts written in the fourteenth century” a sentence of its own, but a clause beginning with “Although” cannot stand alone; it is a fragment.

B.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two main clauses, but “Although the stories survive in manuscripts written in the fourteenth century” is a dependent clause.

D.why_wrong: Without a comma, the introductory clause runs straight into the main clause, “many of them are thought to be much older.”

items.notes: Subject: literature (the Mabinogion, eleven medieval Welsh prose tales preserved in the White Book of Rhydderch and the Red Book of Hergest, fourteenth century, with older oral roots). Real subject the writer knows; no fact-check (WAVE.md). Easy shape of 1.8 (Although clause, period / semicolon / comma / no mark).

items.subtype: Embedded question: statement word order and a period
items.passage: Sundogs are bright spots of light that sometimes appear on either side of the Sun. For centuries, observers wondered how ______ Today, scientists know that sundogs form when sunlight is bent as it passes through flat, six-sided ice crystals drifting in the air.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “How such spots could form” is an embedded question: it serves as the object of “wondered” inside a statement. An embedded question takes statement word order (subject “such spots” before the verb “could form”), and because the whole sentence is a statement, it ends with a period.

A.why_wrong: The sentence reports what observers wondered; it does not ask a question, so question word order (“could such spots form”) and a question mark are both incorrect.

C.why_wrong: The period is correct, but the embedded question needs statement word order (“such spots could form”), not question word order.

D.why_wrong: The word order is correct for an embedded question, but the sentence as a whole is a statement, so it should end with a period, not a question mark.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (sundogs, or parhelia, formed when sunlight is refracted through flat hexagonal plate crystals). Real subject the writer knows; no fact-check (WAVE.md). Easy shape of 1.7: the 2 x 2 grid of word order and end mark in an embedded question after “wondered how.” The modal keeps all four options the same length.

items.subtype: Commas between items of a simple series
items.passage: Over hundreds of thousands of years, winds from the deserts of Central Asia dropped fine yellow silt across north-central China, gradually building up the Loess Plateau. This silt, called loess, makes productive ______ wears away easily, and gives the Yellow River its distinctive color and its name.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The sentence lists three things loess does: it “makes productive farmland,” “wears away easily,” and “gives the Yellow River its distinctive color and its name.” A comma correctly separates the first item from the second in this simple series.

B.why_wrong: A semicolon separates items in a series only when the items themselves contain commas; these simple verb phrases are separated by commas, as the comma after “easily” shows.

C.why_wrong: A colon would introduce “wears away easily ...” as an explanation of “makes productive farmland” rather than separate the first item in the series from the second.

D.why_wrong: Without a comma, “makes productive farmland wears away easily” runs the first two items of the series together.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (the Loess Plateau, wind-blown silt from Central Asian deserts; the Yellow River takes its color and name from the loess it carries). Real subject the writer knows; no fact-check (WAVE.md). Easy shape of 1.12: three verb phrases, blank after the first.

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses: period before a subject
items.passage: In northern New Mexico, many farmers still share water through acequias, communal irrigation ditches first dug during the Spanish colonial ______ acequia is run by its members, who each year elect a mayordomo, or ditch boss, to distribute the water fairly during the growing season.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The first sentence ends with “during the Spanish colonial era.” The second sentence, “Each acequia is run by its members, who each year elect a mayordomo ...,” is a complete main clause with its own subject and verb. A period correctly separates the two sentences.

A.why_wrong: The comma joins the main clause “each acequia is run by its members” to the first main clause with only a comma, a comma splice.

B.why_wrong: With no punctuation or conjunction, the two main clauses are fused into a run-on sentence.

C.why_wrong: When a coordinating conjunction joins two main clauses this long, a comma is conventionally placed before it.

items.notes: Subject: history and social science (acequias of northern New Mexico, communal ditches dating from the Spanish colonial era, run by members who elect a mayordomo). Real subject the writer knows; no fact-check (WAVE.md). Easy shape of 1.14: the second sentence opens with its subject; menu of 1.14 (fused, splice, conjunction without comma).
